Vignette: A 60-year-old man with insulin-dependent diabetes and severe peripheral arterial disease presents with a malodorous toe ulcer with purulent discharge. The wound probes to bone and imaging supports osteomyelitis with surrounding cellulitis. Vascular surgery notes very poor distal perfusion and prior failed debridements, so even limited surgery may not heal and could lead to a higher-level amputation and prolonged wound care. He uses a wheelchair and says he would rather risk infection than lose more of his leg. He refuses debridement and asks to leave. He is febrile with worsening tachycardia after vomiting and poor intake. His mental status fluctuates. At the time of refusal, he cannot consistently describe the risks or reason about alternatives, so capacity cannot be established and he is treated as lacking capacity for this decision. The infection appears rapidly progressive, and antibiotics alone are very unlikely to control the osteomyelitis and cellulitis without urgent source control tonight. No surrogate is reachable. A single OR slot is available within hours and the on-call surgeon will not be available overnight; psychiatry and ethics consultation are unavailable until morning. Hospital counsel confirms either course is legally permissible.
Choice 1: Proceed with urgent operative source control under sedation despite his refusal
Choice 2: Defer surgery tonight and treat medically while reassessing capacity in the morning

Vignette: A 55-year-old man is evaluated in the ED after intentional self-poisoning with an anticoagulant rodenticide. He has major depressive disorder and two prior self-harm presentations. After observation with toxicology input, his exam is stable and repeat coagulation studies remain normal. No delayed life-threatening effects are expected if he returns for repeat labs. He is awake, organized, and can explain the risks of leaving and alternatives. He requests discharge and refuses voluntary psychiatric admission. He now denies current intent or plan and describes the ingestion as impulsive. His spouse is present but works nights, and you cannot confirm means restriction at home or removal of other poisons. Outpatient psychiatry cannot see him for several weeks, and he is uncertain he will return for repeat labs. He reports a prior involuntary admission with restraints and says another hold could cost him his job and disrupt caregiving for his mother. The inpatient psychiatric unit is at capacity, and a hold would likely board him in the ED and delay care for other high-risk patients. Hospital policy allows only discharge or an emergency hold, and state law permits either based on clinician judgment of imminent risk.
Choice 1: Place him on a 72-hour involuntary psychiatric hold for evaluation.
Choice 2: Discharge after medical clearance with a safety plan and urgent follow-up arranged.

Vignette: A 28-year-old woman with chronic migraine enrolled in your optional research study that included ApoE genotyping. The consent said results are usually not returned, but participants may be contacted if a finding seems important. It did not define which findings qualify. Her research-grade report shows an ApoE variant associated with increased Alzheimer risk, but it does not predict whether she will develop dementia. There is no proven prevention plan based on this result alone. She recently asked whether genetics could affect her plans to start a family and to join a prevention registry. She says she wants to know any relevant genetic findings before she moves tomorrow. Her chart notes episodes of health anxiety after unexpected test results. Confirmatory clinical testing and genetic counseling cannot be arranged before she leaves. She has declined portal messaging and you will not have reliable contact after today. Without learning this now, she may make near-term family-planning or registry decisions without the information and later feel harmed or misled. The IRB-approved protocol and institutional policy allow clinician discretion to disclose or not disclose with documentation.
Choice 1: Tell her the ApoE result today
Choice 2: Do not disclose the ApoE result and document your decision

Vignette: A 20-year-old man is seen in an HIV clinic after a new positive test done in jail. He feels well and has decision-making capacity. He agrees to same-day rapid-start ART and wants to become undetectable. He reports recent condomless sex with multiple partners, sometimes during substance use. He is not willing to commit to condoms or abstinence. He brought a handwritten contact list to help remember partners’ names. He allows you to verify spellings, but he refuses any assisted or mediated partner notification. He fears serious personal consequences, including losing housing and possible retaliation, if partners are approached and the disclosure is traced back to him. He is scheduled for release tomorrow and plans to leave the area with no reliable phone. ART will reduce transmission risk, but viral suppression takes time. Partners could have ongoing exposure before suppression. HIV case reporting is complete. Counsel confirms either approach is legally permissible. The health department can only begin outreach if you send the contacts today.
Choice 1: Maintain confidentiality today and initiate ART with risk-reduction counseling.
Choice 2: Forward partner contacts to the health department today for confidential partner services.

Vignette: A 22-year-old man is brought in after a motor vehicle crash with a subdural hematoma and brain contusions. He is intubated and sedated and lacks decision-making capacity. CT and exam suggest rising intracranial pressure. Neurosurgery advises decompression tonight. Delaying until morning could leave him with irreversible neurologic injury. His other bleeding has been controlled and his blood pressure is stable. Transfusion might not be needed, but it could become necessary if hemorrhage is difficult to control. His parents are the default surrogates and refuse any donor blood products as Jehovah’s Witnesses. They report he recently began attending services and told them he would refuse blood even if it meant dying, but he never completed paperwork. A friend says he was considering the faith but was not committed. A court order cannot be obtained in time, and hospital counsel says either course is legally permissible under local emergency and surrogate standards.
Choice 1: Proceed with decompression and authorize transfusion if clinically required intraoperatively.
Choice 2: Proceed with decompression under a strict no-transfusion order, even if exsanguinating.

Vignette: A 58-year-old man is admitted with improving community-acquired pneumonia. At shift change, the nurse reports brief central chest tightness with nausea that has now eased. His vital signs are stable and oxygenation is unchanged. The ECG is already ordered but will not print for about 10 minutes, and the nurse cannot start the chest-pain protocol without a physician order. He does not meet criteria for a rapid response call. No other doctor is on the ward, and the on-call registrar is reliably expected within 5–10 minutes. You are the outgoing junior doctor. You are markedly fatigued and past duty hours, and you will be hard to reach once you leave. If this is acute coronary syndrome, even a short delay in antiplatelet therapy, anticoagulation, and monitoring could increase the risk of infarct extension, malignant arrhythmia, or death. Activating the protocol would also trigger continuous monitoring and possible transfer. Telemetry beds and transfer capacity are near capacity, so activation would likely consume a scarce resource. The treatment could expose him to harm if symptoms are non-cardiac and assessment is mistaken. Hospital policy and counsel confirm that either immediate initiation or documented deferral with prompt handover is acceptable for a stable patient.
Choice 1: Stay, assess now, review the ECG, and activate the chest-pain protocol.
Choice 2: Repeat vitals, document, and hand over for on-call assessment without activating the protocol.

Vignette: A 27-year-old Black woman delivers her first child after an uncomplicated labor. The newborn is well. Both parents report sickle cell disease in close relatives and think they may carry the trait. They refuse the routine newborn blood spot screen for sickle cell status. They report prior involvement of child protective services and past discriminatory experiences. They fear that genetic results in the electronic record can trigger added CPS scrutiny or insurance or employment discrimination, which they believe disproportionately affects Black families. They accept standard exams and vaccines. You explain that many infants with sickle cell disease look well at birth. You note that the screen can be indeterminate and still needs confirmatory testing, but early knowledge can speed counseling, infection-prevention planning, and hematology follow-up. You also note that the state newborn screening program is designed to ensure all infants, especially those at higher risk, have equal access to early sickle cell interventions. The lab cannot hold or de-identify specimens, and results auto-populate the chart. The family plans to leave within hours to a remote area and will not return for outpatient testing soon. Hospital policy and state rules permit either honoring documented refusal or ordering the test over objection after rapid ethics review. Specimens must be sent before the next pickup.
Choice 1: Document refusal and do not send newborn sickle cell screening.
Choice 2: Order and send newborn sickle cell screening despite parental refusal.

Vignette: A 7-year-old girl is brought from a school trip after a fall onto her wrist. X-rays show a displaced, comminuted distal radius fracture. She is neurovascularly intact. Pain improves with IV analgesia, but the deformity remains. The orthopedist recommends reduction soon because delay until tomorrow afternoon may make closed reduction harder due to swelling and can increase long-term stiffness or need for open reduction. ED procedural-sedation staff are not available overnight, so the plan is closed reduction and casting in the operating room under anesthesia. The teacher has a permission form for routine care that excludes anesthesia and is not a legal guardian. You have tried both parents, listed emergency contacts, and the school administrator, and no one is reachable. Overnight splinting and analgesia are feasible but will not correct displacement. An OR team is available now; the next slot is tomorrow afternoon. Hospital policy and counsel advise that either proceeding under an urgent-treatment exception with documentation or waiting for parental consent is legally permissible. You must decide tonight.
Choice 1: Perform closed reduction and casting tonight under an urgent-treatment exception with two-physician documentation
Choice 2: Splint, treat pain, admit overnight, and reduce tomorrow after a parent consents

Vignette: A 58-year-old woman with advanced, progressive multiple sclerosis and diabetic kidney disease is hospitalized for worsening uremia. She is intermittently confused and somnolent, and although she can answer some questions, the team is concerned she currently lacks full decision-making capacity due to uremia and hyperkalemia. She has a longstanding DNR/DNI and an advance directive that declined long-term dialysis, but it did not address a single emergency session. Today her potassium is markedly elevated with ECG changes. She has received IV calcium, insulin with glucose, and inhaled beta-agonist, but the effect is expected to be temporary. The team needs a plan during this shift. Nephrology can place a temporary dialysis catheter and start urgent hemodialysis today. A single session can potentially correct potassium, improve uremia, and may restore her decision-making capacity, but it could lead to ongoing dialysis dependence. Without dialysis, she is likely to die from recurrent hyperkalemia or arrhythmia within hours to days.
Choice 1: Place a temporary dialysis catheter and start urgent hemodialysis
Choice 2: Do not place a catheter or start dialysis and transition to comfort-focused care

Vignette: An 8-year-old child is seen in primary care for prominent auricles and school-related distress after repeated peer comments about his ears. His parents request elective otoplasty. He is developmentally typical and can meaningfully assent or withhold assent. He says he wants the teasing to stop. He is scared of anesthesia and does not want his ears touched now. He is otherwise healthy, with no hearing concerns. The GP reviews that otoplasty is elective. It can cause pain, infection, scarring, visible asymmetry, or later revision, and it may not end teasing. A family history of keloid scarring raises concern about cosmetic outcome. Otoplasty can improve self-esteem for some children with prominent ears. The school will start an anti-bullying plan. A child psychologist can see him within two weeks, but the impact on distress may take time and is uncertain. A visiting surgeon has limited clinic slots this month, shared across children including medically necessary cases. Otherwise the earliest consult is about a year. The GP must decide today whether to refer now or defer referral.
Choice 1: Refer now for elective otoplasty consultation
Choice 2: Defer otoplasty referral and start counseling and school-based supports

Vignette: A 29-year-old woman is starting IVF. Her husband is a carrier of the BRCA variant and they request preimplantation genetic testing for monogenic disease (PGT‑M) to transfer only embryos without the BRCA variant. While the couple is healthy, they wish to avoid passing on a 50% risk of a high-penetrance cancer syndrome.You are the advising physician for a public insurer with a legally capped budget. Standard PGT-M is usually reserved for "severely medically impairing" conditions—typically fatal, early-onset diseases. You must decide whether to grant the exception.
Choice 1: Grant an exception and proceed with IVF plus PGT‑M selection.
Choice 2: Authorize only standard IVF without PGT‑M selection.

Vignette: An 87-year-old woman has a biopsy-confirmed, small, localized invasive ductal breast cancer detected on screening mammography. She lives independently but has severe COPD and limited mobility, using a walker outside the home. She has decision-making capacity. For this presentation, mastectomy and lumpectomy with radiation have similar long-term survival. Anesthesia estimates that mastectomy carries a high risk of perioperative pulmonary complications, with a substantial chance of postoperative ICU admission, prolonged ventilation, and dialysis or pressor support. Lumpectomy is a shorter, lower-risk operation that does not usually require ICU-level care. Postoperative radiation would require several weeks of daily visits and may cause fatigue and skin toxicity, but is medically safer in the short term. The patient states she will only consent to mastectomy and refuses lumpectomy or radiation under any circumstances. The surgeon believes lumpectomy with radiation is the safer and more proportionate option, while mastectomy poses immediate, substantial risk and would likely require scarce ICU resources without a clear survival advantage. Hospital policy permits either proceeding with patient-requested surgery or declining to operate when the risk–benefit balance is unfavorable. The surgeon must decide how to proceed.
Choice 1: Proceed with mastectomy as requested, accepting high perioperative risk and likely ICU use
Choice 2: Decline mastectomy and offer lumpectomy with radiation as the only surgical option.

Vignette: A 48-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer and brain metastases is bedbound and receives tube feeds after recent neurologic decline. She cannot speak full sentences. She consistently answers yes/no. She understands the plan and demonstrates decision-making capacity. She is due for an inpatient chemotherapy infusion in 48 hours. She clearly indicates today that she wants to proceed and does not want to switch to a comfort-only plan. Two months ago, the same regimen led to temporary tumor shrinkage and fewer headaches. Oncology advises that any further symptom stabilization is uncertain and likely limited. The last cycle caused severe nausea and confusion, and her liver tests are now borderline. There is concern for serious toxicity, hospitalization, or sedation that could reduce her remaining alert time. If chemotherapy is canceled, her headaches and neurologic symptoms are expected to worsen within weeks despite steroids and opioids. The drug is compounded off-site in a fixed dose and must be authorized today. It cannot be delayed, modified, or replaced in time. The hospital is experiencing a temporary shortage of this medication. Palliative care is already involved either way. Hospital policy and state law allow either proceeding or canceling in this setting.
Choice 1: Proceed with the scheduled chemotherapy infusion.
Choice 2: Cancel chemotherapy and continue symptom-focused care only.

Vignette: An 84-year-old woman is in the ICU with septic shock from suspected bowel perforation. She is intubated and on vasopressors. After two days of broad-spectrum antibiotics and resuscitation, her lactate is improving but she still needs pressor support and has worsening kidney failure. She opens her eyes to pain but does not follow commands. CT shows a contained perforation that might be operable. The surgeon thinks surgery could control the source, but the risks include perioperative death and prolonged ventilator and dialysis dependence, with an uncertain chance of returning to interactive function. She lacks decision-making capacity. There is no written advance directive or appointed proxy. Her adult children report she opposed long-term dependence on machines, but they cannot relate those statements to a time-limited trial for a potentially reversible illness. If support is withdrawn, she is expected to die in the near term with medications to prevent distress. The ICU and dialysis services are at capacity. Ethics review confirms either course is legally permissible. The team must choose between emergent surgery with full ICU support or comfort-focused withdrawal.
Choice 1: Withdraw ventilator and vasopressors and provide comfort-focused care.
Choice 2: Proceed with emergent surgery and continue full ICU life support.

Vignette: A 25‑week premature newborn remains intubated 48 hours after delivery-room resuscitation for respiratory distress syndrome. She is hemodynamically stable on moderate ventilator support. She has no current sepsis, necrotizing enterocolitis, or uncontrolled bleeding. Cranial ultrasound shows bilateral grade IV intraventricular hemorrhages. The team explains that she could survive the NICU course, but survival may involve severe long‑term neurodevelopmental impairment and ongoing medical dependence, and the exact degree is uncertain this early. To stay ventilated safely she has needed frequent blood draws and suctioning and intermittent analgesia. Today she will either need a new central line for nutrition and medications with a continuous opioid/benzodiazepine infusion, or she will need to be extubated. A time‑limited trial and transfer have been discussed but are not feasible on this timeline. The parents request continuation of all life-sustaining treatment. Several clinicians worry the ongoing procedures and sedation are disproportionate. Hospital policy and state law permit either course.
Choice 1: Place the central line and continue mechanical ventilation with ongoing intensive NICU care
Choice 2: Extubate today and provide comfort-focused care in the NICU

Vignette: A 37-year-old woman with unexplained infertility has tried to conceive for six years. She is using injectable gonadotropins with timed intercourse. Today’s ultrasound shows four mature follicles and several intermediate follicles. Her hormone levels are higher than typical for this protocol. This response raises concern for a multifetal pregnancy, which can increase maternal complications and preterm neonatal morbidity. Pregnancy is still uncertain, and some clinicians proceed in borderline cycles after counseling while others cancel to limit the chance of multiples. She says she accepts the possibility of multiples and, for religious reasons, would not consider selective fetal reduction. After reviewing the risks and alternatives, she requests proceeding tonight. Canceling would mean losing her last authorized, affordable cycle because her coverage ends next month and she cannot take more time off work until then. The ovulation trigger is due tonight. The IVF lab cannot accommodate conversion this cycle, and there is no time for additional monitoring or dose adjustment. Clinic policy and state law allow either approach in this situation.
Choice 1: Give the trigger and proceed with timed intercourse this cycle
Choice 2: Withhold the trigger, cancel the cycle, and advise abstinence or barrier contraception

Vignette: A 57-year-old man with advanced ALS is followed in clinic. He uses a power wheelchair and needs help eating and taking pills. He can still swallow and clearly communicates his goals. He requests medical aid in dying and wants to proceed while he can still self-administer. When alone, he reiterates that he wants aid in dying and explains he fears becoming “a burden” because his wife reports caregiver strain. When she is present, he looks to her before answering questions. State law and hospital policy permit either participation or nonparticipation. An outside referral cannot be completed before his hand strength is expected to decline, so if you decline he will likely lose access.
Choice 1: Proceed with aid-in-dying protocol in your practice and prescribe the medication
Choice 2: Decline to prescribe aid-in-dying medication and enroll him in hospice care

Vignette: A 26-year-old graduate student is in outpatient psychotherapy for severe major depression. Today he reports persistent homicidal ideation toward an identifiable former partner. He names her but gives no time or place. He denies intent to act, denies substance use, and has no history of violence. He reports recently acquiring a weapon and says he could access her when she returns to campus for classes tomorrow. He explicitly refuses you contacting campus security or the former partner. He says he will leave immediately and will not go for emergency evaluation if confidentiality is not maintained. He refuses hospitalization and says any disclosure will end treatment and likely trigger campus discipline and loss of his student visa. The former partner is also a student and is unaware of the risk, so she cannot take precautions unless informed. You can offer a same-day emergency psychiatric evaluation, but mobile crisis cannot arrive before he leaves, and in your jurisdiction an involuntary hold requires stated imminent intent, which he continues to deny. Clinic leadership confirms that either urgent escalation of care with confidentiality or a limited protective disclosure is legally permissible. You must decide before he leaves the office.
Choice 1: Maintain confidentiality today and arrange same-day emergency psychiatric evaluation.
Choice 2: Disclose minimum necessary information today to campus security and the identified person.

Vignette: A 68-year-old man with long-standing paranoid schizophrenia and diabetes is admitted with rapidly worsening necrotizing infection and osteomyelitis of the left foot and ankle. He is febrile and hypotensive despite IV antibiotics and repeated bedside debridement. Vascular surgery says a below-knee amputation could control the source. He is septic with poor circulation, and the stump may not heal. He may need prolonged ventilation and could still die. The ICU team believes he is unlikely to survive without definitive source control in the next day or two. He refuses amputation. He can describe that he could die without surgery and that he would lose the leg with surgery. He insists staff are part of a plot to “harvest” him. He also cites a lifelong religious belief that major body parts must remain intact, confirmed in old clinic notes. Psychiatry and the surgical team disagree on whether fixed delusions prevent him from applying the information to himself. He has no surrogate or advance directive, and he will likely need sedation within hours. Emergency court review is not feasible. Proceeding over objection would require treating him as lacking decision-making capacity, while not amputating would treat him as having capacity and honor his refusal and religious objection.
Choice 1: Perform urgent below-knee amputation, treating him as lacking decision-making capacity
Choice 2: Do not amputate; continue intensive antibiotics and debridement, escalating supportive care as needed

Vignette: A 62-year-old man is admitted for jaundice. Endoscopic biopsy of a pancreatic mass shows adenocarcinoma. He is medically stable, alert, and demonstrates decision-making capacity. He has repeatedly asked you to review the biopsy results today and states he wants to know them even if his brother cannot be present. Over the last 24 hours he has had two witnessed panic episodes with hyperventilation and near-syncope that required PRN lorazepam and a temporary 1:1 sitter. You are concerned that immediate disclosure could precipitate another severe episode with risk of injury or need for restraints. Earlier in the admission he told a nurse he wanted his brother present for bad news. A family meeting is scheduled late this afternoon and is the only time his brother can attend before the patient is transported early tomorrow for staging imaging that requires informed consent. Psychiatry cannot evaluate him until tomorrow morning. Delaying disclosure may postpone consent, staging, and treatment planning. Risk management notes that either immediate disclosure or a documented short delay for acute safety with disclosure within 24 hours is permissible.
Choice 1: Disclose the pancreatic cancer diagnosis to the patient today at the family meeting.
Choice 2: Delay full disclosure until tomorrow after psychiatry evaluation, while telling him results are back.

Vignette: An 18-month-old girl is seen for a well visit. She has never been immunized and has no known contraindications. Her mother refuses all vaccines today and declines a staged schedule. She requests written documentation of her decision. The child is scheduled to return to a large daycare in a few days because the parent cannot arrange other childcare. The clinic has received a notice that a child in her classroom has been diagnosed with measles, and exposures are still being investigated. You explain that measles can cause severe illness in young children and that being unvaccinated increases risk after exposure. You offer same-day catch-up vaccination, referral to a public-health vaccine clinic, and guidance on temporary exclusion and post-exposure prophylaxis if indicated. The mother refuses all of these and says she will still send the child, so the child will likely return unprotected and without exclusion or prophylaxis. A child protective report would likely trigger an immediate assessment that could enforce temporary exclusion and/or facilitate prophylaxis. State law and clinic policy permit either approach, and neither is mandated. You must decide before completing today’s visit.
Choice 1: Continue care, document refusal, and keep offering vaccination and exposure guidance
Choice 2: File a child protective report to assess neglect threshold in this context

Vignette: A 34-year-old woman with a renal transplant 3 years ago requests embryo transfer after IVF for longstanding infertility. She now has stable graft function with no recent rejection. Her blood pressure is controlled on medication. Her ovarian reserve has been poor despite high-dose stimulation, and this cycle yielded only two borderline-quality blastocysts. Both embryos have been thawed for transfer and cannot be refrozen, so they must be transferred within hours or discarded. She strongly prefers transferring both to maximize the chance of pregnancy now because she may not be medically able or financially covered to attempt another cycle. Transplant nephrology and maternal–fetal medicine have counseled that a twin gestation would increase the risk of severe pre-eclampsia, preterm delivery, and graft loss. Hospital policy and state law permit either transfer plan with informed consent.
Choice 1: Transfer both thawed embryos today.
Choice 2: Transfer one thawed embryo today and discard the other.

Vignette: A 72-year-old man fell, and developed an acute subdural hematoma that was evacuated emergently. He has been mechanically ventilated for 10 days. He remains unresponsive. His exam is limited by sedatives needed for ventilator synchrony. Brain MRI shows diffuse injury concerning for hypoxic-ischemic damage. ENT and GI can place a tracheostomy and feeding tube today. The next opportunity is weeks away, and the ICU will not continue prolonged translaryngeal intubation. His wife is the legal surrogate. There is no advance directive, and past comments include both “don’t keep me on machines” and “do everything if there’s a chance.” Neurocritical care estimates a very low likelihood of meaningful neurologic recovery. A tracheostomy and feeding tube would add procedural risks and likely require weeks of ICU care with high risk of complications. Forgoing them would likely lead to death within days after extubation with comfort-focused care. The ICU is at capacity and procedural slots are scarce. An interdisciplinary review has occurred without consensus, and hospital policy and state law allow either course in this situation.
Choice 1: Proceed with tracheostomy and feeding tube and keep him full code
Choice 2: Forgo tracheostomy and feeding tube and transition to comfort care with DNR

Vignette: A 32-year-old woman is in the trauma ICU after a motor vehicle crash. She has been intubated for several days. She remains unable to follow commands when sedation is lightened. The team anticipates prolonged ventilatory support. By tomorrow, they must decide whether to proceed with tracheostomy and feeding tube placement or continue endotracheal ventilation for a short, time-limited period and reassess. Both options are medically reasonable but differ in invasiveness and long-term burden. She has no advance directive and no documented proxy. Her husband is reachable and requests to serve as surrogate. He says he knows her preferences from prior hospitalizations. Her parents report a recent separation and alleged intimate partner violence. A prior emergency visit note documents suspected IPV involving the husband. The parents report she previously told them she would want them, not her husband, to make decisions if she lacked capacity. The IPV concern raises safety and coercion risks if the husband controls consent and access. Hospital policy prioritizes a spouse but allows an alternate-surrogate process when there is credible concern about appropriateness. The hospital has applied this process inconsistently in IPV-suspected cases, raising fairness concerns. Counsel confirms either route is legally permissible. A court-appointed guardian cannot be obtained in time, and the ICU requires one surrogate to consent now.
Choice 1: Contact the husband and designate him as surrogate decision-maker now.
Choice 2: Initiate the alternate-surrogate process and designate the parents as surrogates now.

Vignette: A woman in her 70s with end-stage pulmonary fibrosis is seen on an urgent home visit for acute worsening dyspnea. She can only speak in short phrases. Her SpO2 stays low despite her usual home oxygen regimen and nebulizers. She is febrile with a new cough, raising concern for a potentially reversible infection or mucus plugging on top of her chronic disease. Earlier today, while still clearly alert, she said she would accept a short ICU “trial,” including possible intubation, if there were a reversible problem, but she did not want prolonged life support. There is no POLST or written directive. Over the next hour she becomes drowsy and intermittently confused, and you cannot reliably confirm her wishes. Her family requests full life-prolonging treatment if she worsens, and no one is clearly designated as surrogate. Prior pulmonology notes state that if she is intubated, liberation from the ventilator would be unlikely given her baseline disease. The ICU is near capacity and a ventilator would be a scarce resource. If she stays home, she could die within hours to days, and you have limited medications to control severe air hunger.
Choice 1: Arrange ambulance transfer and pursue hospital-based life-prolonging treatment, including intubation.
Choice 2: Continue home-based symptom management and do not arrange hospital transfer.

Vignette: A 30-year-old man with advanced AIDS is admitted for fever, profound cachexia, and progressive shortness of breath. He has severe kidney failure on chronic kidney disease with volume overload and rising potassium. IV diuretics, potassium binders, and dietary restriction have helped only partially. He is awake, consistent, and judged to have decision-making capacity. He has a documented DNR/DNI and has declined further invasive diagnostic testing and blood transfusion. Nephrology explains that intermittent hemodialysis is technically possible but requires immediate placement of a large central venous catheter and an ongoing schedule. They cannot offer a one-session or time-limited trial. After hearing this, he still requests dialysis to gain time and clarity to be home with his child, and hospice-only care would conflict with this preference. Dialysis may relieve uremic dyspnea and confusion, but it could cause hypotension, bleeding without transfusion backup, line infection, and ICU-level escalation he does not want. Without dialysis, he has high short-term risk of fatal arrhythmia and worsening uremia despite maximal medical therapy. Dialysis staffing is critically limited, and only one catheter and dialysis slot remain tonight under a triage policy prioritizing potentially reversible illness. A plan is needed before the slot closes.
Choice 1: Place a dialysis catheter and start scheduled inpatient intermittent hemodialysis.
Choice 2: Forego dialysis and provide medical management with hospice-directed symptom care.

Vignette: A 27-year-old woman with HIV is 18 weeks pregnant and comes to prenatal care with her male partner. She is usually engaged in care but recently missed doses, and her last viral load was detectable. She has not told him her diagnosis. They have condomless sex, and she says he wants to try to conceive again soon. She reports concern for retaliation if he learns her status, though she describes no prior physical assaults. A social worker is available today, but she refuses assisted disclosure. She asks you not to imply HIV or recommend testing without a specific concern. Local law and hospital policy permit either approach.
Choice 1: Disclose her HIV diagnosis to the partner and arrange urgent testing.
Choice 2: Keep her status confidential.

Vignette: A 15-year-old girl is seen in your adolescent medicine clinic with both parents. Her father has Huntington’s disease and has early symptoms. She requests predictive testing before moving for a new school term in three weeks. She reports panic, insomnia, and falling grades from the uncertainty. Her parents support the request and are willing to provide consent. She has a past episode of depression but denies current suicidal thoughts. You assess her as able to explain the test, its limits, and possible long-term consequences. Her mental health clinician expects that having a result could substantially reduce her current symptoms and help her plan supports for the move. A positive result would not change medical care now. Early testing may also cause lasting anxiety or depression, regret, or stigma and discrimination. If testing is deferred, her current symptoms may persist and worsen school functioning. The regional genetics service discourages testing under 18 but will consider a mature-minor exception with a physician’s order today. If you do not submit it now, testing is unlikely for at least a year due to transfer of care and insurance change.
Choice 1: Refer for genetics counselling and order predictive Huntington testing now
Choice 2: Provide counselling and defer predictive Huntington testing until age 18

Vignette: A 56-year-old man is seen in neurology for two years of worsening memory, wide-based gait, and new urinary urgency with incontinence. MRI shows findings consistent with NPH. He can explain the purpose and risks of a shunt in his own words. He gives a stable reason for refusal, citing a longstanding aversion to implanted devices, but he is intermittently disoriented and cannot describe how refusal affects his fall and driving risks. He refuses admission in any setting. His spouse is the usual surrogate but is reluctant to consent against his stated wishes, and asks you to help her decide. Involuntary admission could require restraints or sedation and may trigger delirium and lasting loss of trust. Honoring refusal is expected to forgo potential benefit. Hospital counsel confirms that either course is legally permissible.
Choice 1: Respect his refusal and arrange outpatient monitoring and safety supports.
Choice 2: Pursue involuntary admission.

Vignette: A 28-year-old healthcare assistant presents to occupational health for unit-specific clearance today. She works on a cardiology step-down unit where many patients are at high risk for respiratory complications and often cannot mask. The hospital is under a temporary infection-control directive after a recent influenza-like illness cluster on the unit. She declines the influenza vaccine. She is offered vaccine declination under policy and is informed that declining may require temporary reassignment during outbreaks; she still refuses. Policy and the union agreement allow declination with added precautions, and they also allow occupational health to restrict staff from high-risk units and arrange reassignment during an outbreak; counsel confirms either approach is legally permissible. Masking and symptom screening reduce risk but are not fully protective. The unit is already critically understaffed. Reassigning her would require mandatory overtime for the remaining staff and raise the risk of fatigue-related errors. No additional float or replacement staff are available without pulling from other understaffed services. The director wants a decision before finalizing this week’s schedule.
Choice 1: Clear her for the step-down unit with masking and daily symptom attestation
Choice 2: Deny step-down clearance and require other staff to cover her shifts

Vignette: A 44-year-old woman is seen in your breast clinic for cancer-risk management. Her mother and two maternal aunts had premenopausal breast cancer. A multigene panel found no pathogenic variant, and no affected relative is available for confirmatory testing. Genetics considers her pedigree very high risk, but her exact risk remains uncertain. She has followed a high-risk program for years with alternating MRI and mammography every 6 months. Despite CBT and an SSRI trial, she has persistent anticipatory anxiety that disrupts sleep and work and has led to urgent visits; she has started postponing imaging and fears she will stop screening. She requests bilateral prophylactic mastectomy, which would be expected to substantially reduce breast-cancer risk but not eliminate it. She has decision-making capacity and has met with plastic surgery about optional reconstruction and possible numbness, chronic pain, body-image or sexual changes, and the possibility of re-operations. State law and hospital policy permit either approach.
Choice 1: Schedule bilateral prophylactic mastectomy, with optional immediate reconstruction.
Choice 2: Do not schedule surgery now; continue enhanced surveillance and mental-health treatment.

Vignette: A 35-year-old woman is in the ICU after a massive intracranial haemorrhage. She conceived with IVF after infertility and was 23 weeks pregnant when she was found unresponsive. Death by neurologic criteria has been confirmed by two physicians per protocol. She has no written advance directive, and her spouse is the legal surrogate. Ultrasound shows a reassuring fetal heart rate and no anomalies. Neonatology says a live birth would require weeks of physiologic support and the neonatal outcome is uncertain. The spouse requests continued ventilation and escalating ICU interventions and reports the patient had explicitly stated that if she were declared brain-dead while pregnant, she would want life support continued for fetal benefit. Her sister recalls a general wish to avoid prolonged machine support, but they never discussed pregnancy or neurologic death. Ongoing interventions cannot benefit the patient and would require vasopressors, transfusions, invasive lines, and possibly dialysis, with rising risks of infection and bleeding. If support is withdrawn, fetal demise is expected within minutes to hours. The ICU is at capacity and blood products are limited. You must decide today whether to escalate or withdraw.
Choice 1: Continue somatic support and fetal surveillance with intent to prolong gestation.
Choice 2: Withdraw ventilatory and circulatory support and provide comfort-focused care.

Vignette: A 28-year-old man is in the ICU after a motor vehicle crash and has been declared dead by neurologic criteria following standard testing. Mechanical ventilation is being continued temporarily. His driver’s license documents intent to be an organ donor. In this hospital, organ donation may proceed either based on documented donor intent alone or after family authorization; both approaches are permitted. His parents state they do not want donation pursued today and ask for more time, despite acknowledging his donor designation, and they do not wish to meet with donation staff at this time. Donation evaluation must begin soon to preserve organ viability. Proceeding now would honor the patient’s expressed wishes and may benefit transplant recipients but would go directly against the parents’ stated opposition and risk significant harm to trust and the grieving process. Waiting until tomorrow would respect the parents’ request but may make donation impossible and undermine the patient’s autonomous decision. The team must decide how to proceed.
Choice 1: Proceed with organ donation evaluation today based on the patient’s documented donor intent
Choice 2: Defer donation evaluation until tomorrow in deference to the parents’ request.

Vignette: A 16-year-old with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia achieved remission after induction and consolidation. She is now starting maintenance therapy. Your center is enrolling patients in an IRB-approved trial comparing two commonly used maintenance durations, 2 years versus 3 years, using the same drugs and doses. Clinicians disagree about whether the added year meaningfully lowers relapse risk or mainly adds cumulative toxicity and disrupts adolescent development. Her mother provided permission and the patient assented. Randomization assigns her to 3 years. She says she would not have agreed if she knew she could be assigned longer treatment. She strongly prefers 2 years because ongoing fatigue, nausea, frequent clinic visits, and infection precautions are already straining school and friendships despite supportive care. You worry that pressing the longer plan could damage trust and adherence. You also worry that the trial is near its minimum enrollment target and is already underpowered, so post-randomization withdrawals could waste scarce research slots and funding and delay evidence that will guide care for many future leukemia patients. State law and hospital policy permit either continuing or withdrawing from research. Pharmacy needs the maintenance orders finalized before the next cycle.
Choice 1: Keep her enrolled and proceed with the three-year maintenance assignment.
Choice 2: Withdraw her from the study and prescribe a two-year maintenance schedule.

Vignette: A 30-year-old woman with known HIV returns after years without care. She has oral candidiasis and unintentional weight loss. She is afebrile and comfortable. She denies dyspnea, severe headache, focal neurologic symptoms, or confusion. Faxed records show prior advanced immunosuppression with a CD4 count below 50 and panic attacks after distressing medical discussions, including an ED visit. She arranged childcare for one hour and asks you not to discuss prognosis or “how bad it is” today. She says she will not agree to blood draws unless you explain in detail what tests could show and what the results would mean, even if that discussion increases her anxiety. Baseline staging labs today would guide ART timing, opportunistic infection prophylaxis, and urgent screening for occult infections such as cryptococcal disease. Delaying labs for several days could postpone this planning and miss a treatable complication. The clinic social worker can meet with her only in 72 hours, which may reduce panic and improve follow-up. Hospital policy allows either proceeding today or deferring with documented refusal.
Choice 1: Explain your concern today and obtain baseline HIV staging labs now.
Choice 2: Defer staging discussion and labs today and bring her back in 72 hours.

Vignette: A 14-year-old boy is on an adolescent psychiatry unit for severe behavioral dysregulation and is diagnosed with adjustment disorder with mixed disturbance of emotions and conduct. He is in seclusion after repeated assaultive behavior toward staff. For the past 48 hours he has taken only a few supervised sips and has refused meals. When drinks or food are brought into the room he sometimes grabs and throws them, and staff have been struck during attempts to retrieve items. He is awake and oriented but highly impulsive. He repeatedly states he will not drink or eat even if it makes him sick. The team is divided about whether he can meaningfully refuse hydration right now. Nursing notes dry mucous membranes and increasing dizziness on standing, though vital signs remain acceptable. His legal guardian is reached by phone and asks staff to avoid force unless medical deterioration is clear. Risk management has approved only two overnight protocols with current staffing. A plan is needed before the night shift.
Choice 1: Initiate involuntary IV hydration, with restraints and intramuscular sedation as needed
Choice 2: Continue offering oral intake without force and monitor closely for medical deterioration

Vignette: A 44-year-old woman is in outpatient psychiatry for her fourth visit. She reports two years of intrusive suicidal ideation that worsens during conflict at home. Today she denies intent to act and denies a near-term plan. She says she has access to lethal means at home but agrees to lock them away and complete a written safety plan. She is not intoxicated and has no psychosis. You judge her short-term suicide risk as moderate because of chronic suicidal ideation and access to lethal means, despite her denial of intent. She refuses antidepressants and declines voluntary ED evaluation, voluntary hospitalization, and an intensive outpatient program. She also refuses permission to contact her spouse or any other support person. She reports a prior involuntary hold as traumatic and says she may stop coming if it happens again. The visit is ending and you cannot arrange earlier follow-up or same-day mobile crisis. Hospital policy and state law allow either approach when imminence is uncertain.
Choice 1: Discharge with enhanced safety plan and keep her disclosures confidential
Choice 2: Initiate emergency involuntary psychiatric evaluation today despite her refusal

Vignette: An 18-month-old girl receives routine intramuscular immunizations per schedule after you confirm no contraindications. Later the same day, you notice a charting discrepancy suggesting she may have received the same set of vaccines at a visit the prior week. If a duplicate dose occurred, most children do well, but fever or marked local swelling can develop overnight. Earlier parental monitoring, antipyretics, or urgent evaluation could reduce complications and could affect how future vaccines are timed. The mother has a documented history of severe health anxiety that has led to repeated unplanned ED visits and stopping vaccines after alarming news. Immediate disclosure could trigger another ED visit or stopping all future vaccines. She has also asked that medical issues not be left on voicemail, and she is not answering calls today; the only way to reach her before close is a brief portal message that may be read without support. If you wait, you can confirm the immunization registry and lot numbers and arrange a nurse call tomorrow morning with clear triage guidance, but delaying disclosure could delay evaluation if the child develops fever or swelling overnight. The clinic has limited nurse triage capacity, and avoidable after-hours ED use strains shared resources. Risk management advises that either immediate portal disclosure or a documented, time-limited delay for verification and planned disclosure is legally permissible. You must decide before end of day.
Choice 1: Send a portal message today disclosing the possible duplicate vaccine dose.
Choice 2: Delay disclosure until a planned call tomorrow after verifying the immunization record.

Vignette: A 38-year-old woman is seen in outpatient psychiatry for escalating workplace conflict and longstanding suspiciousness. Over four visits you have documented prominent paranoid personality traits, rapid anger when feeling criticized, and a prior episode in which she filed multiple retaliatory complaints after reading a critical evaluation. Today she arrives upset but becomes calm during the visit. A focused suicide risk assessment finds intermittent passive death wishes without intent, plan, or preparatory behavior, and she agrees to a safety plan and follow-up. She demands to log into the patient portal and read your signed progress notes alone before leaving. She refuses an in-session note review and says any delay will be “proof” you are hiding misconduct. The note includes your impression of "paranoid traits," descriptions of tense interactions, and collateral details from her HR file. Similar unsupervised access to critical documentation has previously led to marked escalation, including retaliatory actions and worsening suicidal thoughts. You believe reading these notes now is likely to acutely worsen her paranoia and anger and increase risk of self-harm or retaliatory behavior. She also needs documentation for an HR grievance due tomorrow. IT cannot provide supervised or partial access, and the note is locked unless you place a time-limited hold. Your clinic generally provides same-day note access to all patients to support equitable transparency. Compliance confirms either approach is permissible under policy and applicable law. A brief clinical summary would meet the HR deadline while reducing the chance of destabilization and therapeutic rupture.
Choice 1: Provide same-day portal access to the full signed progress notes
Choice 2: Place a time-limited hold and provide a brief written clinical summary

Vignette: A 12-year-old boy is seen with his mother for a brief post-hospital follow-up after abdominal pain; symptoms have resolved. His exam again shows severe pediatric obesity with stage 1–2 hypertension, without headache, chest pain, or other end-organ symptoms. When weight is mentioned, he becomes visibly panicked and hyperventilates. He says he was recently bullied at school and asks not to discuss weight today. He asks to speak privately, but his mother insists you tell him to diet and refuses to step out. In the hospital he had panic symptoms when staff discussed his size, and his mother reports he sometimes skips meals afterward. Screening questions raise concern for emerging disordered eating behaviors. He has acanthosis nigricans, and hospital labs showed worsening ALT compared with prior records, suggesting evolving metabolic disease. The family drove several hours and is unlikely to return for 6–12 months. The clinic cannot provide telehealth, and the family does not reliably use phone or portals. Pediatric guidance supports addressing obesity over time but allows deferring sensitive counseling when distress or eating-disorder risk is a concern. Deferring counseling today may delay evaluation of progressive metabolic disease; initiating counseling may worsen panic or disordered eating. You have only a few minutes to decide what to do next.
Choice 1: Initiate weight-focused counseling and place obesity-clinic and nutrition referrals today
Choice 2: Complete hospital follow-up and hypertension plan, deferring all weight counseling and referrals

Vignette: A 50-year-old woman is referred for long-standing grief and depression after the deaths of two children. She lives alone and has withdrawn from supports. She reports persistent anhedonia, guilt, insomnia, and daily thoughts that life is not worth living. Over several visits, she consistently requests assisted dying. She states she refuses further psychiatric treatment, including structured complicated-grief therapy or neuromodulation. She denies suicidal intent outside the assisted-dying pathway and reports no acute plan or preparatory behaviors. Years ago she had a nonfatal overdose after a bereavement. She previously completed several antidepressant trials and supportive therapy, and she stopped them due to side effects and no relief. Two consultants find she can understand, appreciate, reason, and communicate a stable choice. They disagree on whether additional evidence-based treatments offer a meaningful chance of improvement. Assisted dying would end her suffering but is irreversible. Intensive treatment could require hospitalization and exposes her to medication side effects and restrictive monitoring. Hospital counsel confirms either course is legally permissible. The committee meets in two days, and without your recommendation the application closes for months.
Choice 1: Submit endorsement for assisted dying and prescribe life-ending medication per protocol.
Choice 2: Decline to endorse assisted dying and arrange voluntary intensive psychiatric treatment.

Vignette: An 86-year-old man with no terminal illness requests physician-assisted dying. He is independent in daily activities and demonstrates decisional capacity. He consistently explains that long-held beliefs about dependence and loss of meaning make his ongoing life intolerable. Over the past year he tried a senior center and brief bereavement counseling but stopped, saying they worsened his distress. He will accept a one-time family meeting and home safety planning, but refuses ongoing therapy. He has set a date two weeks away and says he may attempt self-harm if you decline. He agrees he is not in immediate danger today and will remove lethal means and accept daily check-ins. In this jurisdiction, enduring existential suffering can meet eligibility if confirmed by psychiatry and two physicians. Hospital counsel affirms either proceeding or declining is permissible. Initiating could relieve his enduring suffering and reduce risk of a violent self-harm attempt. It also involves prescribing lethal medication and proceeding despite concern for potentially treatable depression or complicated grief. Declining avoids direct iatrogenic death and medication-related harms. It may prolong severe distress and leave him at higher risk of unsupervised self-harm. The required second physician can review this week, but will not assume care unless you initiate the process, and paperwork must be signed within days.
Choice 1: Initiate the physician-assisted dying process after required second-physician confirmation
Choice 2: Decline assisted dying and provide intensive supportive care with close follow-up

Vignette:
A 32-year-old man with profound intellectual disability lives in a long-term care facility. He is nonverbal with no known prior wishes, no family, and a court-appointed guardian. He is hospitalized with newly diagnosed aggressive acute leukemia with adverse features. Induction is unlikely to be curative, but it could produce a remission for months and allow return to his facility with fewer transfusions and fewer hospital transfers. It requires a central line and weeks of inpatient care with daily labs. He becomes agitated with procedures and may need limited 1:1 staffing or temporary safety measures to protect the line. Without induction, clinicians expect survival to be markedly shorter with rising risks of bleeding and infection that may be difficult to control in the facility despite transfusions.

The leukemia unit is at capacity with a waitlist for induction beds and 1:1 sitters. Blood products are also limited due to a regional shortage, and induction would require frequent transfusions. The team must decide within days because delay may make him too unstable for induction. Hospital policy and state law permit the guardian to consent to or refuse this treatment under a best-interest standard.
Choice 1: Proceed with induction chemotherapy and inpatient monitoring with central venous access
Choice 2: Decline chemotherapy and provide transfusions as tolerated with comfort-focused care

Vignette: A 7-year-old boy presents 45 minutes after a fall with a full-thickness laceration through the upper lip crossing the vermilion border. There is mild dirt contamination but no tissue loss, avulsion, oral commissure involvement, facial nerve deficit, or parotid duct concern. His tetanus shots are up to date. He is stable but very anxious and will likely need procedural sedation for a careful layered closure. No in-house ENT or oral surgery coverage is available tonight. You are the on-call general surgeon and are credentialed and experienced in layered lip repairs. Either you or a plastic surgeon can achieve an acceptable functional repair. Plastics may offer a modest cosmetic advantage and a lower risk of vermilion misalignment or noticeable scarring. A plastic surgeon is available from home and can arrive in about an hour. Waiting means prolonged fasting and distress. It also increases swelling and may require deeper sedation. The on-call plastic surgeon is also covering multiple facilities and other emergencies, and activating after-hours call-in uses limited specialist resources and overtime costs that can delay other patients’ care. Hospital policy and state law permit either plan with parental consent. The parents want the best appearance but also want the repair done soon.
Choice 1: Activate after-hours plastics call-in for definitive layered repair
Choice 2: Perform definitive layered repair yourself in the ED tonight

Vignette: A woman in her early 50s with progressive multiple sclerosis is admitted to the high-dependency unit with depressed consciousness after suspected ingestion of acetaminophen and opioids. She is wheelchair-dependent and needs help with most daily care, but she had been communicating reliably before this event. She was intubated on arrival before staff could locate her paperwork. Two years ago, during a neurology admission, she signed a witnessed advance decision refusing CPR and “ICU ventilation and other invasive life support” if her MS reached a stage of irreversible decline; she described wanting to avoid prolonged ventilation and tracheostomy. The document does not mention self-poisoning or short-term treatment for an acute, potentially reversible illness. She now has worsening liver injury. Clinicians think she has a good chance of hepatic recovery with immediate antidotal therapy and organ support, but deterioration could still lead to a prolonged ICU course with ongoing invasive support. Her husband asks for extubation based on the document. Her adult daughter says her mother recently discussed an upcoming family milestone and would accept brief ICU care for reversible problems. Local policy permits temporary life-sustaining treatment while applicability is clarified, and permits withdrawal if it is judged applicable. The physician must decide within hours.
Choice 1: Continue ventilation and ICU organ support while initiating definitive antidotal treatment
Choice 2: Withdraw ventilation and stop escalation, transitioning immediately to comfort-focused end-of-life care

Vignette: A 19-year-old man traveled from abroad to serve as a non-directed living kidney donor through your hospital’s established transplant program. He is healthy and compatible within the program’s matching pathway. He has completed the standard medical workup, psychosocial evaluation, and independent donor advocate interviews. In several private interviews he consistently states he has wanted to donate since adolescence and denies being offered money. His mother and stepfather are concerned and warn that his religious community expects members to donate and that refusal can bring serious social consequences. When asked directly about pressure, he avoids discussing his community. He says he can refuse if he wants and still wants to proceed. Hospital counsel confirms that either proceeding or declining is legally permissible.  The nephrectomy is scheduled in four days, and his visa and return flight make rescheduling impractical. You must decide today.
Choice 1: Proceed with donor nephrectomy as scheduled.
Choice 2: Decline him as a living donor at this center and cancel surgery.

Vignette:
A 78-year-old man with moderate dementia is hospitalized with aspiration pneumonia and delirium and cannot make medical decisions. Before this illness, he repeatedly told his family that he wanted to avoid extreme medical measures, restraints, or prolonged suffering, even if that meant a shorter life.
He can no longer swallow safely. Doctors can place a PEG (feeding tube through the stomach), but because he pulls at medical lines, doing so would likely require physical restraints or sedating medications, directly conflicting with his stated wishes. PEG placement could prolong his life and allow transfer to a nursing facility while awaiting possible recovery of swallowing function.
If a PEG is not placed, he can be fed small amounts by hand for comfort, accepting that he may receive inadequate nutrition and die sooner. This approach would require prolonged hospitalization with one-to-one nursing care, using limited hospital resources that would otherwise be needed for other seriously ill patients awaiting admission.
The medical team must decide how to proceed.
Choice 1: Proceed with PEG placement for enteral nutrition.
Choice 2: Do not place PEG and implement comfort feeding only.

Vignette:
A 36-year-old man is in the ICU after a motorcycle crash. He has a non-survivable traumatic brain injury. Death is determined by neurologic criteria per protocol, including apnea testing. He remains on the ventilator only for organ support. The organ procurement organization reports he is listed as a donor in an out-of-state registry entered over a decade ago. 
His parents adamantly oppose organ recovery. They claim that while he may have signed up a decade ago, he "wouldn't have wanted this". However, they cannot provide any evidence (such as recent conversations, written notes, or registry withdrawals) to support a change of heart. The OPO says recovery must start within two hours. Several candidates are actively waiting tonight, including a status-1 liver recipient. If recovery is delayed, organs will become nonviable and recipients may die waiting. Hospital counsel confirms that either proceeding or standing down is legally permissible here.
Choice 1: Maintain organ support and initiate surgical organ recovery tonight
Choice 2: Stand down from recovery; discontinue organ support after one hour of bedside time

Vignette: A 38-year-old man with severe autism and profound intellectual disability is brought from his day program for acute behavioral dysregulation with unsafe elopement toward a busy street. He is nonverbal and cannot demonstrate understanding of admission or communicate a consistent choice. No legal guardian or prior documented preferences are available in the chart. His long-term foster carers cannot be reached until the morning. In the ED he is afebrile with stable vital signs. A brief exam shows no obvious trauma or intoxication, but pain, seizure, or medical delirium have not been excluded and labs and observation are pending. After a low-dose sedative and a quiet room, he is calmer but intermittently heads toward exits and becomes distressed with repeated redirection. The ED cannot provide overnight 1:1 observation. Observation status may not legally prevent him from leaving if he calms, increasing elopement and missed workup risk. A statutory involuntary hold would prevent leaving even when calm and provides due-process review, but typically requires locked-door detention and may involve restraints or IM medication. A 1:1 sitter is a limited resource needed for other high-risk patients. The team must choose a pathway tonight.
Choice 1: Admit under time-limited observation status with 1:1 monitoring and least-restrictive precautions.
Choice 2: Initiate a formal involuntary hold and admit under locked-unit detention procedures.

Vignette: A 28-year-old woman is 12 weeks pregnant with her first child. She and her partner both have achondroplasia. They request chorionic villus sampling with targeted FGFR3 testing. You explain that two pathogenic variants are typically lethal shortly after birth, one variant causes achondroplasia with long-term survival, and no variant predicts average stature. They would continue the pregnancy if the fetus has achondroplasia. They would end the pregnancy if the fetus is biallelic (lethal) or has no FGFR3 variant (they say they believe they will connect better to a child that is similar to them). CVS carries a small risk of pregnancy loss, and they accept this risk for timely, actionable results. Results would return while first-trimester termination is still possible, but only if referral is placed now. State law and hospital policy permit both testing and elective termination. Hospital policy requires the ordering clinician to place any requested termination referral to preserve equal access to time-sensitive care. Otherwise you must transfer care. The nearest alternate provider is hours away and cannot see her before the cutoff. Transfer would likely force continuation of a lethal pregnancy or a later, higher-risk procedure. You have a serious moral objection to facilitating termination of an unaffected fetus.
Choice 1: Order CVS with full FGFR3 testing and place a termination referral on request.
Choice 2: Decline participation and urgently transfer obstetric care to another clinician.
